extracted.intended_audience: high school students preparing for the ACT writing (timed essay)
extracted.subtask_description: Explains the ACT Writing scoring rubric (four domains, 1–6 reader ratings), how scores are aggregated, and concrete strategies to raise a timed ACT essay score within 40 minutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas and Analysis (Domain 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generates productive ideas and engages critically with multiple perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Graders look for whether you simply restate the given perspectives or develop your own nuanced position. A score of 6 means you offered precise, complex thinking that examines implications. A score of 4 means your analysis was clear but stayed at a surface level without exploring deeper connections. Move from restating to critically engaging opposing perspectives, acknowledging merits and tensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Development and Support (Domain 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explains, explores, and illustrates ideas with reasoning and examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-scoring essays don't just assert a position — they explore implications, provide specific examples, and explain why their reasoning leads to their conclusion. A score of 6 shows skillful development with genuine depth, while a score of 4 relies on adequate but basic support. The domain is often the key differentiator between average and high scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization (Domain 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arranges ideas with clarity and purpose and uses transitions to guide the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At a score of 6, every paragraph has a clear controlling idea that connects logically to the next, creating a purposeful progression. At a score of 4, the structure is workable and recognizable (introduction-body-conclusion) but may lack sophistication in transitions or sequencing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language Use and Conventions (Domain 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrates control of word choice, sentence structure, grammar, punctuation, and style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Score-6 responses show effective, varied language choices with strategic sentence structure and minimal errors; score-4 responses show competent language with some variety and minor errors. Important: factual accuracy is NOT graded on the ACT essay. Using complex vocabulary incorrectly can hurt your score more than using simple words correctly. Audience awareness matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-reader scoring process and discrepancy resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Two trained readers independently score each essay on a 1–6 scale per domain; if their scores for any domain differ by more than one point a third trained reader resolves the discrepancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each reader has less than five minutes to score an essay, so clarity, structure, and quickly obvious argumentation matter. Neither reader sees the other's scores before submitting their own evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain score aggregation and final writing score calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Each domain score is the sum of both readers' ratings (2–12); the final subject-level writing score is the rounded average of the four domain scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Domain scores (2–12) are reported; the final writing score is reported separately from the ACT composite score of 1–36. The writing score contributes to the ELA score when combined with English and Reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Score-level descriptors (1–6 per reader)
rubrics_metrics.description: Numeric reader-level scale where 6=Effective, 5=Well-Developed, 4=Adequate, 3=Developing, 2=Weak, 1=Little or No Skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 6: Demonstrates effective skill in writing an argumentative essay with nuance and precision. 5: Shows well-developed skill with clear reasoning and purposeful organization. 4: Displays adequate skill with clear ideas and workable structure but limited depth. 3: Shows some developing skill with partial understanding and inconsistent support. 2: Demonstrates weak or inconsistent skill with minimal engagement. 1: Shows little or no skill in writing an argumentative essay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual accuracy is not scored
rubrics_metrics.description: Graders evaluate writing quality, argumentative skill, and use of evidence — not whether specific facts or statistics are correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on crafting a strong argument and clear reasoning rather than memorizing or attempting to prove factual claims; incorrect facts do not directly lower scores, but poor integration of evidence or reasoning can.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan before you write (pre-writing and time management)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spend dedicated planning time before drafting to identify a thesis and outline body paragraphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended 40-minute plan: Minutes 1–2: read the prompt and perspectives; identify agreements/conflicts. Minutes 3–7: plan essay, choose position, outline 2–3 body paragraphs and which perspectives to engage. Minutes 8–33: write following the outline (focus on depth over length). Minutes 34–37: review for clarity and paragraph-thesis connections. Minutes 38–40: proofread for grammar, spelling, and punctuation. Planning prevents loss of Organization and Ideas & Analysis points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage critically — avoid mere summary
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not simply summarize the three perspectives; develop your own position and address counterarguments logically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why opposing perspectives have limitations rather than ignoring them. Use specific examples and reasoning (not just assertions). A common mistake is writing a generic five-paragraph essay without a nuanced thesis — the rubric rewards critical thinking and depth over formulaic structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the rubric as a revision checklist (proofreading priorities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reserve several minutes at the end to check Organization, Development, and Language Use against rubric expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Save 3–5 minutes to ensure each paragraph connects to the thesis (Organization), that specific examples are included (Development and Support), and that sentence structures vary (Language Use). Fixing a few grammar errors or unclear transitions can raise scores by a point in those domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: ACT Essay self-check checklist (concrete production criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: A short list of explicit production items students should verify before submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Items (as given on the page): I stated a clear, specific thesis that goes beyond restating a given perspective; I addressed at least two of the three provided perspectives; Each body paragraph includes specific reasoning or examples; I explored implications, not just stated opinions; My essay has a clear introduction, body, and conclusion; Transitions connect my paragraphs and ideas logically; I varied my sentence structures and word choices; I proofread for grammar, spelling, and punctuation.
